nameStory: The red mulberry gets its name from the deep reddish-purple color of its ripe fruits, which distinguish it from its white mulberry cousin. The word 'mulberry' comes from the Old English 'morberie,' originally derived from Latin 'morum,' meaning the mulberry fruit that has been prized by humans and wildlife for centuries.
description: Red mulberry is a medium-sized native tree that typically grows 20-40 feet tall with a rounded, spreading crown. It's part of the same family as figs, and like its relatives, produces sweet, juicy fruits that look like elongated blackberries. The tree has broad, heart-shaped leaves that can be smooth-edged or deeply lobed, sometimes even on the same branch. Red mulberry is becoming increasingly rare in New England, making any sighting special.

idTips.label: Fruit
idTips.description: Dark red to purple aggregate fruits that look like elongated blackberries, about 1 inch long. They're sweet and juicy when ripe, with a texture similar to blackberries but growing directly from branches rather than canes.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Heart-shaped leaves that feel rough and sandpapery on top, soft underneath. They can be unlobed, mitten-shaped with a thumb, or deeply three-lobed, sometimes all on the same tree. Leaves turn bright yellow in fall.

idTips.label: Bark
idTips.description: Grayish-brown bark that becomes furrowed with age, developing long, scaly ridges. Young branches are smooth and reddish-brown.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Medium-sized tree with a broad, rounded crown and spreading branches. Often found as isolated specimens rather than in groves.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny greenish flowers appear in spring in drooping clusters called catkins. Male and female flowers are usually on separate trees, though some trees have both.

habitat: Red mulberry prefers rich, moist soils in floodplains, along streams, and in fertile woodlands. In New England, it's most likely found in southern areas, often in partially shaded locations or forest edges. It thrives in areas with good drainage but consistent moisture.

seasonality.spring: Small greenish flower clusters appear in May before or with the emerging leaves. The rough-textured, heart-shaped leaves unfurl and can show their variable lobing patterns.
seasonality.summer: Fruits ripen from red to dark purple in July and August, becoming sweet and attracting birds and other wildlife. Leaves are fully mature and show their distinctive sandpaper-like texture.
seasonality.fall: Leaves turn bright golden-yellow before dropping. Fruits are gone by now, but fallen fruit stains may still be visible on the ground beneath trees.
seasonality.winter: Bare branches show the tree's spreading growth habit. Buds are small and reddish-brown, and the furrowed bark pattern is most visible.

funFact: Red mulberry trees can live over 100 years and were so valued by early American settlers that they tried to establish a silk industry using the leaves to feed silkworms - the same way silk had been made in Asia for thousands of years with white mulberry leaves.
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with the invasive white mulberry, but red mulberry has rough, sandpapery leaves (white mulberry's are smooth and glossy) and darker, more flavorful fruit. Remember: 'Red mulberry = rough leaves, white mulberry = smooth and shiny.'
contextualKnowledge: Red mulberry is actually quite rare in New England and is considered endangered in Canada due to habitat loss and hybridization with the non-native white mulberry. Many 'mulberry' trees people encounter are actually the introduced white mulberry, making true red mulberry sightings particularly noteworthy for conservation.
compareHints: Red mulberry differs from white mulberry by its rougher, sandpaper-textured leaves and deeper-colored, more flavorful fruits. White mulberry has smooth, glossy leaves and lighter-colored fruits that are often less sweet. Korean mulberry is rarely encountered in New England but has smaller leaves and fruits than either red or white mulberry.

relatedSpecies.distinction: White mulberry differs from native red mulberry by its glossy, waxy-feeling leaves (versus red mulberry's rough, sandpapery leaf undersides) and more extreme leaf shape variation on individual trees.
Korean mulberry is distinguished from white mulberry by its rougher, more sandpapery leaves and longer, more cylindrical fruits.
